title: 10-week Applied AI / ML engineer plan
summary: Coding patterns and system design first, then either applied AI or ML engineering, ending with two full mock loops. About 8–10 hours a week.

rhythm.text: Two coding problems by pattern: 25 minutes to solve, 10 to review, then rewrite one from memory.
System design reading and a one-page design note.
One 45-minute mock (coding or design) with a written debrief, then a 15-minute weekly review and error-log update.

rules: Talk out loud while you solve, as you would in the interview.
State the time and space complexity before you code.
Test edge cases: empty input, one item, duplicates, and the largest size.
Log every miss with why it happened and the fix.

python: collections.Counter counts in one pass, and defaultdict(list) groups without checking for missing keys.
Use collections.deque for queues: popleft() is O(1), while list.pop(0) is O(n).
heapq is a min-heap on a plain list. Push (priority, item) tuples, and negate the priority for a max-heap.
bisect_left and bisect_right binary-search a sorted list for you.
sorted(items, key=lambda r: (r[1], -r[0])) sorts by several keys. list.sort() sorts in place and returns None.
Recursion stops at about 1,000 frames by default. Use an explicit stack for deep trees and graphs.
Integers never overflow, and float("inf") is a clean starting minimum.
typescript: Use Map and Set for lookups and counts: keys keep their type, and size and insertion order come built in.
There is no built-in heap. Write a small binary heap (an array with sift-up and sift-down) that takes a comparator.
There is no deque. For a BFS queue, keep an array and a head index; shift() can cost O(n).
sort() compares as strings by default: [10, 9, 1].sort() gives [1, 10, 9]. Pass (a, b) => a - b for numbers.
Numbers are 64-bit floats, exact up to Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER (2^53 − 1). Use BigInt beyond that, and Math.floor for integer division.
Type the signature first, e.g. function topK(nums: number[], k: number): number[], and narrow nullable nodes before using them.
Infinity and -Infinity are clean starting values for a minimum or maximum.

tip.python: Counter(nums) and defaultdict(list) cover most counting and grouping. Key anagram groups by "".join(sorted(word)).
tip.typescript: Count with a Map: counts.set(x, (counts.get(x) ?? 0) + 1). Plain objects turn keys into strings. Key anagram groups by [...word].sort().join("").

weeks.focus: Stacks for nesting and next-greater questions, binary search on sorted data and on the answer, and prefix sums for range totals.

tip.python: A list is a stack: append, pop and stack[-1]. bisect_left finds the first index whose value is not less than the target. list(accumulate(nums, initial=0)) builds prefix sums.
tip.typescript: An array is a stack: push, pop and stack.at(-1). Write binary search yourself, with Math.floor((lo + hi) / 2) for the midpoint. Prefix sums go in an array of length n + 1 that starts at 0.

tip.python: BFS: deque([start]) with popleft(). Sort intervals with ranges.sort(key=lambda r: r[0]). Dijkstra: heapq with (distance, node) tuples, skipping stale entries.
tip.typescript: BFS: an array queue with a head index. Sort intervals with ranges.sort((a, b) => a[0] - b[0]). Dijkstra needs your own heap, or an O(V²) scan for small graphs.

tip.python: Build grids with [[0] * cols for _ in range(rows)]; [[0] * cols] * rows repeats one shared row. Greedy orderings usually start with sort(key=...).
tip.typescript: Build grids with Array.from({ length: rows }, () => new Array(cols).fill(0)); new Array(rows).fill(row) shares one row. Pass a comparator to every numeric sort.
